cd3b90ec934f: The student speaks fluently, so start from what they already know: “Which cases do you use without thinking?”. The goal of the lesson is not something new but a system: one map for all the cases.
c10c06d0eea2: Even fluent speakers say “nie mam samochód” out of habit — check by ear. Only the accusative changes (and “jest → nie ma”).
02e42c3c3831: The main trap is «z»: where from (dopełniacz / genitive) vs with whom or what (narzędnik / instrumental); English uses two different words, from and with. Ask for a pair: z pracy / z kolegą.
d4ee3eed7a38: Ask “gdzie? / dokąd?” about each example. English “at the beach / to the beach” works the same way, so the student hears the difference — we make it a system.
804ef981576a: The logic «location → narzędnik (instrumental), movement → biernik (accusative)» for five prepositions. Ask the student to translate a pair of sentences in mirror image.
5bd02b1df422: Key point: the biernik (accusative) of animate nouns = dopełniacz (genitive) — studenta; of inanimate nouns = mianownik (nominative) — komputer. Miejscownik (locative): -e with a consonant change (studencie, stole) or -u after soft consonants (lekarzu).
8244d8db09d9: It is a tendency, not a law: komputera, but samochodu, telefonu. A student who already speaks should trust their ear and check doubtful forms in a dictionary.
e19f3a6cce30: In letters, at work, with strangers — wołacz (vocative) only. «Kasia, chodź!» is fine among friends, but «Pani Anna, proszę…» sounds careless.
8dc533aa4ca9: The student most likely already uses these forms by ear — just name them as a separate group. The third point is the colloquial norm; in a formal text «wysłać e-mail» is more common.
7aff0964c08e: Two groups in -ę (imię → imienia, zwierzę → zwierzęcia) and nouns in -um, which do not change in the singular.
2181b932562d: Here English has no case at all, while Polish needs the genitive after these verbs. Ask the learner to continue the list: potrzebować, bać się, unikać.
